source_text: Τὸ δὲ ἴδιον καὶ ταὐτὸν τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐσίᾳ καὶ ἐξ αὐτῆς γέννημα φύσει τυγχάνον τί ἂν εἴη, ἢ πάλιν καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο ὁμοούσιον τῷ γεννήσαντι; τοῦτο γὰρ Υἱοῦ πρὸς Πατέρα γνώρισμα. Καὶ ὁ μὴ τοῦτο λέγων, οὐ φρονεῖ, φύσει καὶ ἀληθῶς Υἱὸν εἶναι τὸν Λόγον. Οὕτω νοήσαντες οἱ Πατέρες, ἔγραψαν ὁμοούσιον εἶναι τὸν Υἱὸν τῷ Πατρὶ, καὶ ἀνεθεμάτισαν τοὺς λέγοντας ἐξ ἑτέρας ὑποστάσεως εἶναι τὸν Υἱόν· οὐχ ἑαυτοῖς πλασάμενοι λέξεις, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτοὶ ἀπὸ τῶν πρὸ αὐτῶν Πατέρων μαθόντες, καθάπερ εἴπομεν. Τούτων δὲ οὕτω δεικνυμένων, περιττὴ αὐτῶν ἡ Ἀρίμηνος, περιττὴ καὶ ἡ ἄλλη παρ' αὐτῶν ὀνομαζομένη περὶ πίστεως σύνοδος. Ἀρκεῖ γὰρ ἡ ἐν Νικαίᾳ σύμφωνος οὖσα καὶ τοῖς ἀρχαίοις ἐπισκόποις, ἐν ᾗ καὶ οἱ Πατέρες αὐτῶν ὑπέγραψαν, οὓς αἰδεῖσθαι τούτους ἔπρεπεν, ἵνα μὴ πάντα μᾶλλον ἢ Χριστιανοὶ νομισθῶσιν. Εἰ δὲ καὶ μετὰ τοσαῦτα, μετὰ καὶ τὴν μαρτυρίαν τῶν ἀρχαίων ἐπισκόπων, καὶ μετὰ τὴν ὑπογραφὴν τῶν ἰδίων Πατέρων, προσποιοῦνται, ὡς ἀγνοοῦντες, τὴν λέξιν φοβεῖσθαι τοῦ ὁμοουσίου, εἰπάτωσαν καὶ φρονείτωσαν ἁπλούστερον μὲν καὶ ἀληθῶς τὸν Υἱὸν φύσει Υἱὸν, ἀναθεματισάτωσαν δὲ, ὡς παρήγγειλεν ἡ σύνοδος, τοὺς λέγοντας κτίσμα, ἢ ποίημα, ἢ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, ἢ, Ἦν ποτε ὅτε οὐκ ἦν ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ· καὶ ὅτι τρεπτὸς καὶ ἀλλοίωτός ἐστι, καὶ ἐξ ἑτέρας ὑποστάσεως· καὶ οὕτω φευγέτωσαν ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀρειανῆς αἱρέσεως· καὶ θαῤῥοῦμεν, ὅτι γνησίως ταῦτα ἀναθεματίζοντες ὁμολογοῦσιν εὐθὺς, ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας καὶ ὁμοούσιον εἶναι τὸν Υἱὸν τῷ Πατρί. Διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ οἱ Πατέρες, εἰρηκότες ὁμοούσιον εἶναι τὸν Υἱὸν, ἐπήγαγον εὐθύς· Τοὺς δὲ λέγοντας κτίσμα, ἢ ποίημα, ἢ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, ἢ, Ἦν ποτε, ὅτε οὐκ ἦν, ἀναθεματίζει ἡ Καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία· ἵνα διὰ τούτων γνωρίσωσιν, ὅτι ταῦτα σημαίνει τὸ ὁμοούσιον. Καὶ ἡ τοῦ ὁμοουσίου δύναμις γινώσκεται ἐκ τοῦ μὴ εἶναι κτίσμα ἢ ποίημα τὸν Υἱόν· καὶ ὅτι ὁ λέγων ὁμοούσιον οὐ φρονεῖ κτίσμα εἶναι τὸν Λόγον· καὶ ὁ ἀναθεματίζων τὰ προειρημένα ὁμοούσιον ἅμα φρονεῖ εἶναι τὸν Υἱὸν τῷ Πατρί· καὶ ὁ ὁμοούσιον λέγων γνήσιον καὶ ἀληθινὸν λέγει τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ. Καὶ ὁ Γνήσιον λέγων νοεῖ τό· Ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ Πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν· καὶ, Ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἐμὲ ἑώρακε τὸν Πατέρα. Ἔπρεπε μὲν οὖν διὰ πλειόνων τὰ τοιαῦτα γράφειν· ἐπειδὴ δὲ πρὸς εἰδότας ὑμᾶς γράφομεν, διὰ τοῦτο συντόμως ὑπηγορεύσαμεν· εὐχόμενοι παρὰ πᾶσι σώζεσθαι τὸν σύνδεσμον τῆς εἰρήνης, καὶ πάντας τοὺς τῆς Καθολικῆς Ἐκκλησίας τὸ αὐτὸ λέγειν, τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν. Καὶ οὐχ ὡς διδάσκοντες, ἀλλὰ ὡς ὑπομιμνήσκοντές ἐσμεν. Ἐσμὲν δὲ οὐχ ἡμεῖς οἱ γράφοντες μόνοι, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντες οἱ ἐν τῇ Αἰγύπτῳ καὶ ταῖς Λιβύαις ἐνενήκοντά που ἐπίσκοποι. Πάντων γὰρ ἕν ἐστι τοῦτο φρόνημα, καὶ ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων ἀεὶ ὑπογράφομεν, ἐὰν συμβῇ τινα μὴ παρεῖναι. Οὕτως οὖν διακείμενοι, ἐπειδὴ συνέβη συνελθεῖν ἡμᾶς, ἐγράψαμεν καὶ τῷ ἀγαπητῷ ἡμῶν Δαμάσῳ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ τῆς μεγάλης Ῥώμης περὶ τοῦ Αὐξεντίου τοῦ ἐπελθόντος τῇ ἐν Μεδιολάνῳ ἐκκλησίᾳ, διηγούμενοι τὰ κατ' αὐτόν· ὅτι τε οὐ μόνον τῆς Ἀρειανῆς αἱρέσεώς ἐστι κοινωνὸς, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπεύθυνός ἐστι πολλοῖς κακοῖς, πράξας ταῦτα μετὰ Γρηγορίου τοῦ κοινωνοῦ τῆς ἀσεβείας αὐτοῦ· καὶ θαυμάζοντες πῶς μέχρι νῦν οὐ καθῃρέθη καὶ ἐκβέβληται τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, καὶ χάριν ὡμολογήσαμεν τῇ θεοσεβείᾳ αὐτοῦ τε καὶ τῶν συνελθόντων ἐν τῇ μεγάλῃ Ῥώμῃ, ὅτι καὶ τοὺς περὶ Οὐρσάκιον καὶ Οὐάλεντα, καὶ τοὺς τὰ αὐτὰ αὐτοῖς φρονοῦντας ἐκβάλλοντες, ἔσωσαν τὴν ὁμοψυχίαν τῆς Καθολικῆς Ἐκκλησίας· ἣν καὶ παρ' ὑμῖν εὐχό μενοι σώζεσθαι, παρακαλοῦμεν μὴ ἀνέχεσθαι, καθὰ προείπομεν, τῶν προβαλλομένων ὄχλον συνόδων προφάσει πίστεως, τὴν ἐν Ἀριμήνῳ, τὴν ἐν Σιρμίῳ, τὴν ἐν τῇ Ἰσαυρίᾳ, τὴν ἐν τῇ Θρᾴκῃ, τὰς ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει, τὰς ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ πολλὰς καὶ ἀτάκτους.
thought_title: The Son's proper relation to the Father's substance and the sufficiency of Nicaea
orientation: Athanasius is arguing that the Son is proper to the Father's substance and therefore consubstantial, and that the Nicene creed and its anathemas are sufficient, making later councils unnecessary.
pass_a_gloss: But what would the proper and identical thing to the substance of God and the offspring from it by nature be, or again also according to this consubstantial with the begetter? For this is the mark of the Son in relation to the Father. And the one not saying this does not think that the Word is by nature and truly Son. Having thought thus, the Fathers wrote that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, and they anathematized those saying that the Son is from another actual being; not having fabricated words for themselves, but they themselves also having learned from the Fathers before them, just as we said. But these things being shown thus, their Ariminum is superfluous, superfluous also the other council named by them concerning the faith. For the one in Nicaea is sufficient, being in agreement also with the ancient bishops, in which also their Fathers subscribed, whom these men ought to have respected, so that they might not be considered everything rather than Christians. But if also after so many things, after also the testimony of the ancient bishops, and after the subscription of their own Fathers, they pretend, as being ignorant, to fear the word of the consubstantial, let them say and think more simply and truly the Son by nature Son, and let them anathematize, as the council commanded, those saying creature, or thing made, or from nothing, or, There was when the Son of God was not; and that he is changeable and alterable, and from another actual being; and thus let them flee from the Arian heresy; and we are confident that, genuinely anathematizing these things, they confess immediately that the Son is from the substance and consubstantial with the Father. For because of this also the Fathers, having said that the Son is consubstantial, added immediately: But those saying creature, or thing made, or from nothing, or, There was when he was not, the Catholic Church anathematizes; so that through these things they might make known that these things signify the consubstantial. And the force of the consubstantial is known from the Son not being creature or thing made; and that the one saying consubstantial does not think that the Word is a creature; and the one anathematizing the things said before thinks at the same time that the Son is consubstantial with the Father; and the one saying consubstantial says that the Son of God is genuine and true. And the one saying Genuine understands the: I and the Father are one; and, The one having seen me has seen the Father. It was fitting therefore to write such things at greater length; but since we write to you who know, for this reason we have dictated briefly; praying that among all the bond of peace be preserved, and that all those of the Catholic Church say the same thing, think the same thing. And we are not as teaching, but as reminding. And we are not only we who write, but also all the bishops in Egypt and the Libyas, about ninety. For of all this is one mind, and on behalf of one another we always subscribe, if it happens that someone is not present. Being thus disposed, since it happened that we came together, we wrote also to our beloved Damasus the bishop of great Rome concerning Auxentius who intruded upon the church in Milan, narrating the things concerning him; that he is not only a partaker of the Arian heresy, but also is liable to many evils, having done these things with Gregory the partaker of his impiety; and wondering how until now he has not been deposed and cast out of the Church, and we gave thanks to the piety of him and of those who came together in great Rome, that casting out those around Ursacius and Valens, and those thinking the same things as them, they preserved the unity of mind of the Catholic Church; which also praying to be preserved among you, we exhort you not to tolerate, as we said before, those putting forward a crowd of councils under pretext of faith, the one in Ariminum, the one in Sirmium, the one in Isauria, the one in Thrace, the many and disorderly ones in Constantinople, the ones in Antioch.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'actual being' for hypostasis, and the phrase is the Arian slogan the Fathers anathematized; 'another' preserves the force of heteras.
The word denotes a distinguishing sign or token; 'mark' is concise and literal, fitting the argument that consubstantiality identifies the Son.
The word means excessive or unnecessary; 'superfluous' captures the rhetorical dismissal of Ariminum as redundant.
The verb means to dictate for writing; 'dictated' preserves the epistolary context of a letter composed by dictation.
The compound means same-mindedness; 'unity of mind' is literal and fits the context of preserving Catholic concord.

pass_b_english: But what would it be that is proper to and identical with the substance of God, and is by nature his offspring from that substance, if not again, in this very respect, consubstantial with the one who begot him? For this is the mark of Son in relation to Father. And whoever does not say this does not think that the Word is truly and by nature Son. The Fathers understood it this way, and so they wrote that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, and they anathematized those who say the Son is from another actual being. They did not fabricate words for themselves, but they too learned from the Fathers before them, as we have said.

Since these things are demonstrated in this way, their Ariminum is superfluous, and so is the other council they name concerning the faith. For the council at Nicaea is sufficient, since it agrees also with the ancient bishops, and in it their own Fathers subscribed—men whom these people ought to have revered, so that they might not be considered anything rather than Christians. But if after so much, after the testimony of the ancient bishops and after the subscription of their own Fathers, they pretend, as if ignorant, to fear the word 'consubstantial,' let them say and think more simply and truly that the Son is by nature Son, and let them anathematize, as the council commanded, those who say he is a creature, or a thing made, or from nothing, or 'there was when the Son of God was not,' and that he is changeable and alterable, and from another actual being. And so let them flee from the Arian heresy. And we are confident that, genuinely anathematizing these things, they immediately confess that the Son is from the substance and consubstantial with the Father.

For this reason the Fathers, having said that the Son is consubstantial, immediately added: 'But those who say he is a creature, or a thing made, or from nothing, or there was when he was not, the Catholic Church anathematizes.' They did this so that through these things people might recognize that this is what 'consubstantial' means. And the force of 'consubstantial' is known from the fact that the Son is not a creature or a thing made; and the one who says 'consubstantial' does not think the Word is a creature; and the one who anathematizes the things mentioned above at the same time thinks the Son is consubstantial with the Father; and the one who says 'consubstantial' says the Son of God is genuine and true. And the one who says 'genuine' understands: 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), and 'Whoever has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9).

It would have been fitting to write such things at greater length, but since we are writing to you who know, we have dictated briefly for this reason, praying that the bond of peace may be preserved among all, and that all those of the Catholic Church may say the same thing and think the same thing. And we are not writing as teachers but as those who remind. Nor are we the writers alone, but also all the bishops in Egypt and the Libyas, about ninety in number. For this is the one mind of all, and we always subscribe for one another if it happens that someone is absent.

Being so disposed, since it happened that we were assembled, we also wrote to our beloved Damasus, the bishop of great Rome, concerning Auxentius who intruded upon the church in Milan, relating the facts about him: that he is not only a sharer in the Arian heresy, but is also liable for many evils, having done these things with Gregory, the partner of his impiety. And we expressed amazement that until now he has not been deposed and cast out of the Church, and we gave thanks for the piety of Damasus himself and of those assembled in great Rome, because by casting out Ursacius and Valens and those who think the same things as they do, they preserved the unity of mind of the Catholic Church. And praying that this unity may be preserved also among you, we urge you not to tolerate, as we said before, those who put forward a crowd of councils under the pretext of the faith—the one in Ariminum, the one in Sirmium, the one in Isauria, the one in Thrace, the ones in Constantinople, and the many disorderly ones in Antioch.

problems.quote: the one in Ariminum, the one in Sirmium, the one in Isauria, the one in Thrace, the many disorderly ones in Constantinople and Antioch.
problems.source_quote: τὴν ἐν Ἀριμήνῳ, τὴν ἐν Σιρμίῳ, τὴν ἐν τῇ Ἰσαυρίᾳ, τὴν ἐν τῇ Θρᾴκῃ, τὰς ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει, τὰς ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ πολλὰς καὶ ἀτάκτους.
problems.why: Source has plural 'the ones in Constantinople, the many disorderly ones in Antioch'; English merges both cities under one plural adjective.
problems.fix: the ones in Constantinople, and the many disorderly ones in Antioch.
problems.ruling: Greek: τὰς ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει (plural), τὰς ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ πολλὰς καὶ ἀτάκτους (plural, many disorderly). English wrongly makes 'many disorderly' modify both cities together, obscuring that only Antioch's councils are explicitly called 'many disorderly.'

edits.old: the many disorderly ones in Constantinople and Antioch.
edits.new: the ones in Constantinople, and the many disorderly ones in Antioch.

fixed: Source has 'τὰς ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει, τὰς ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ πολλὰς καὶ ἀτάκτους' — plural 'the ones in Constantinople' and 'the many disorderly ones in Antioch' as separate items; English merged them under one adjective. Fixed.

problems.ruling: Source uses present indicative ὁμολογοῦσιν, not conditional; 'if...will' changes meaning to hypothetical.

last_rejected.quote: the one in Ariminum, the one in Sirmium, the one in Isauria, the one in Thrace, the ones in Constantinople, and the many disorderly ones in Antioch.
last_rejected.source_quote: τὴν ἐν Ἀριμήνῳ, τὴν ἐν Σιρμίῳ, τὴν ἐν τῇ Ἰσαυρίᾳ, τὴν ἐν τῇ Θρᾴκῃ, τὰς ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει, τὰς ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ πολλὰς καὶ ἀτάκτους.
last_rejected.why: Source has plural 'councils' for Constantinople (τὰς) and Antioch (τὰς πολλάς); English singular 'the ones' loses the plural.
last_rejected.fix: those in Constantinople, and the many disorderly ones in Antioch.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'ones' renders plural τὰς; no meaning lost. 'Many disorderly ones' captures πολλὰς καὶ ἀτάκτους.

last_rejected.source_quote: ἵνα μὴ πάντα μᾶλλον ἢ Χριστιανοὶ νομισθῶσιν
last_rejected.why: Greek means 'lest they be considered anything rather than Christians'—a warning. English 'so that they might not be considered anything rather than Christians' misreads ἵνα μὴ as purpose rather than negative result; but more critically, 'anything rather than' is awkward and potentially misreadable. Actually the key issue: the Greek says they should revere the Fathers 'so that they not be considered anything rather than Christians'—the English 'so that they might not be considered anything rather than Christians' is grammatically strained. The sense is 'lest they be thought anything but Christians.' The 'might not' with 'anything rather than' creates confusion about whether it's 'might not be considered [anything rather than Christians]' = might be considered Christians, or 'might not be considered anything, rather than Christians.' The Greek is clear: 'lest they be considered anything rather than Christians' = 'lest they be considered non-Christians.'
last_rejected.fix: lest they be considered anything other than Christians
last_rejected.ruling: ἵνα μὴ + subjunctive is standard purpose; 'so that they might not' correctly renders it. 'Anything rather than Christians' is awkward but not wrong.

last_rejected.quote: we always subscribe for one another
last_rejected.why: ὑπογράφομεν means 'we subscribe/sign' not 'we subscribe for one another' in the sense of representing. The Greek ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων means 'on behalf of one another'—when someone is absent, others sign for them. 'Subscribe for one another' is unclear English; it sounds like they subscribe to each other rather than signing on behalf of absent colleagues.
last_rejected.fix: we always sign on behalf of one another
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων + ὑπογράφομεν = 'subscribe for one another'; context (εἰ μὴ παρεῖναι) clarifies on-behalf-of meaning.
